newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwaiti emir tells parliament to protect secrets.
newsitem.headline: Kuwaiti emir tells parliament to protect secrets.

text.p: Kuwait's emir on Sunday told the first session of the newly elected parliament to protect state secrets.
"No one said that exposing our secrets...is a democratic target," Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah told the only elected Gulf Arab parliament.
"States spend a lot of effort and money to safeguard secrets ...but we volunteer to expose them...thus weakening us in front of enemies and embarrass us with friends," he added.

The last parliament opened probes into alleged official corruption and abuse of state funds and events ahead of Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait. It also questioned some arms deals with Western powers that had helped end the seven-month occupation.
"Criticism is the start of reform, provided that it is criticism and not accusations," added the emir.
Crown Prince and Prime Minister Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah told parliament that Kuwait was committed to plans to rebuild its military after the disaster of the Iraqi invasion.
He said his government, formed on Tuesday, "will continue with efforts to rebuild, rehabilitate, equip and train the Armed Forces to boost its defensive capabilities".

Veteran MP Ahmad al-Saadoun on Sunday narrowly won a third consecutive term as parliament speaker. Jassem al-Kharafi, former finance minister and a member of one of Kuwait's wealthiest families, lost by one vote.
Kharafi later protested that the speaker needed an absolute majority of MPs -- 31 instead of the 30 Saadoun received. One ballot was invalid.
Parliament, the second since the 1991 Gulf War, is made up of 50 elected MPs and 10 government ministers who are ex-officio members with the right to vote.
Parliament was restored in 1992, six years after the emir dissolved it citing security concerns at the height of the nearby 1980-88 Iran-Iraq war.
The new parliament is expected to be less confrontational than the last because pro-government MPs won 19 seats in the election.

There are no political parties in Kuwait but analysts say Shi'ite and Sunni Moslem fundamentalists and pro-Islamists have about 14 parliament seats, six are held by liberals and the rest is shared by independents and tribal candidates.
